prompt: A surprise expense appeared after you made your plan. Which idea best explains why some plans handled it better?

options.text: Plans with some savings kept as a buffer could pay without borrowing.
options.explanation: A buffer turns a crisis into an inconvenience. It is the whole point of keeping a little aside.

options.text: The plans that spent everything were just unlucky.
options.explanation: It was not luck. A surprise is certain to happen sometimes; only the buffer is up to you.

options.text: Borrowing is always the cheapest way to handle a surprise.
options.explanation: Borrowing adds a cost later. Using a buffer first usually costs less.

prompt: Why does a good budget cover needs before wants?

options.text: Needs like transport and food cannot be skipped without real consequences.
options.explanation: Essential costs come first because missing them causes bigger problems than missing a want.

options.text: Wants are always bad and should never be bought.
options.explanation: Wants are fine in moderation. The skill is keeping them in check after needs are safe.

options.text: The order does not matter if the total is the same.
options.explanation: The order matters: if money runs short, the last items are the ones you drop.

prompt: You wanted to save for a goal. What most increased your chance of reaching it?

options.text: Setting aside a fixed amount early in the month, before spending on wants.
options.explanation: Paying your goal first makes saving a habit instead of whatever is left over.

options.text: Hoping there would be money left at the end of the month.
options.explanation: Leftover money is rarely left. Decide the saving first.

options.text: Spending freely and saving only if the goal is cheap.
options.explanation: A plan that depends on what is left over is not really a plan.

prompt: Why keep an emergency fund separate from your goal savings?

options.text: So an emergency does not force you to raid, or give up on, your goal.
options.explanation: Separate pots protect your goal from surprises.

options.text: Because emergencies never happen if you plan well.
options.explanation: Even the best planners face surprises. Planning means being ready.

options.text: Because one big pot always earns more interest.
options.explanation: Interest depends on the rate and time, not on lumping goals together.

prompt: Why does compound interest grow faster than simple interest over time?

options.text: Interest is earned on earlier interest as well as on the original amount.
options.explanation: That 'interest on interest' effect grows bigger the longer the money stays.

options.text: Because the bank pays a higher rate for compound interest.
options.explanation: The rate can be the same. The difference comes from re-earning on past interest.

options.text: Because you must add more money each month.
options.explanation: Compounding happens even without new deposits; time does the work.

prompt: Which habit made the biggest difference to your savings result?

options.text: Saving a regular amount every month and not touching it.
options.explanation: Small regular amounts, left alone, are powerful.

options.text: Saving a very large amount once, then stopping.
options.explanation: Regular saving builds a habit and gives time more to work with.

options.text: Keeping the money in cash at home so it is easy to spend.
options.explanation: Money that is easy to spend tends to get spent.

prompt: Why does spreading money across different baskets reduce risk?

options.text: When one thing falls, others may hold up, so one bad outcome cannot sink everything.
options.explanation: Diversification does not remove risk, but it limits how much one failure can hurt.

options.text: Because every basket always grows at the same rate.
options.explanation: Baskets move differently, which is exactly why mixing them smooths the ride.

options.text: Because single companies are guaranteed to do better.
options.explanation: A single company can fall 40% or more in a year. There are no guarantees.

prompt: If you need money in one year, what is the sensible way to think about risk?

options.text: Choose steadier options, because a fall may not have time to recover.
options.explanation: The shorter the time you have, the less room you have to wait out a fall.

options.text: Choose the riskiest option to grow quickly.
options.explanation: Risky things can lose money fast. Short deadlines need steadier choices.

options.text: Time makes no difference to risk.
options.explanation: Time horizon is one of the most important parts of how much risk is sensible.

prompt: The market fell during your simulation. What is the most useful lesson?

options.text: Falls are normal; what matters is whether you needed the money soon and how calmly you react.
options.explanation: Fictional or real, markets rise and fall. Reacting in panic can lock in losses.

options.text: A fall proves investing is a scam.
options.explanation: Falls are part of how markets behave. They are not proof of a scam.

options.text: You should always sell at the first sign of a fall.
options.explanation: Selling in a panic often turns a temporary fall into a permanent loss.

prompt: Why should you never share an OTP or PIN, even with someone claiming to be from your bank?

options.text: Genuine banks never ask for them; anyone who does is trying to move your money.
options.explanation: OTPs and PINs are keys. They are for you only.

options.text: Because sharing is only risky if the caller sounds rude.
options.explanation: Scammers sound polite and official. The request itself is the red flag.

options.text: Because OTPs are only needed to receive money.
options.explanation: You never need a PIN or OTP to receive money.

prompt: What is the strongest warning sign in a message that says 'Act in 10 minutes or lose your money'?

options.text: Urgency. Scammers rush you so you will not stop to check.
options.explanation: Slow down and verify through an official channel you already trust.

options.text: The message uses capital letters.
options.explanation: Style is a weak clue. Pressure and requests for money or secrets are the strong clues.

options.text: It came on a weekend.
options.explanation: Timing alone does not tell you anything. Pressure does.

prompt: A message promises to triple your money in a month. What should you conclude?

options.text: Guaranteed high returns do not exist; this is a classic scam pattern.
options.explanation: Real investments carry risk. Anyone promising guaranteed big returns is not telling the truth.

options.text: It is probably fine if a friend forwarded it.
options.explanation: Friends can be fooled too. Check the offer, not who passed it on.

options.text: Try it with a small amount first to see.
options.explanation: Small payments are how scams start. Do not send anything.

prompt: By month six the earphones cost more than they did at the start. What does that show?

options.text: Prices rise over time, so money that earns nothing buys a little less later.
options.explanation: That is inflation. Keeping some money in something that earns helps protect buying power.

options.text: The shop made a mistake.
options.explanation: Gradual price rises are normal across the whole economy. It is not a mistake.

options.text: Saving is pointless because prices always win.
options.explanation: Saving still works, especially when your money earns at least something.

prompt: Why did money that was 'kept ready' make the surprise easier?

options.text: It was available instantly with no loss, which is what liquidity means.
options.explanation: Liquid money can be used right away without selling at a bad price or borrowing.

options.text: Cash always earns the most interest.
options.explanation: Cash earns nothing. It is useful for being available, not for growing.

options.text: Surprises only matter if you have no goal.
options.explanation: Surprises can derail any goal. Being ready is how you protect it.

prompt: Why is putting most of the ₹500 in the growth basket risky for a goal six months away?

options.text: A poor period can shrink it, and there may not be time to recover before you need the money.
options.explanation: Short deadlines leave little room to wait out a fall.

options.text: Because the growth basket always loses money.
options.explanation: It can also gain. The point is that it is uncertain, so it suits money you do not need soon.

options.text: Because deposits never lose value to inflation.
options.explanation: Deposits can lose buying power too if their rate is below inflation.
